hero.title: Union and Its Territory
hero.description: Master Part I of the Indian Constitution (Articles 1 to 4)—the foundational provisions defining the territory of India, the power of Parliament to reorganize states, the procedure for boundary alteration, and the evolution of the Indian federation (UPSC GS Paper-II: Constitutional Law).

mockIntro.title: Interactive UPSC Mock Test
mockIntro.description: Assess your understanding of Articles 1 to 4 of the Constitution, state reorganization procedures, landmark Supreme Court rulings (like Berubari Union), and federal boundary committees through a timed test.

timeline.title: Evolution of States & Territories
timeline.description: Key commissions and constitutional milestones in the reorganization of Indian States.

cards.details: Linguistic Provinces Commission appointed by the President of the Constituent Assembly. Recommended reorganization based on administrative convenience rather than linguistic factors.
Committee of Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, and Pattabhi Sitaramayya. Formally rejected language as the basis for reorganization of states.

Three-member commission (Fazl Ali, K.M. Panikkar, H.N. Kunzru) appointed after the creation of Andhra State. Accepted language as a major basis of reorganization but rejected the 'one language-one state' theory.
Enacted by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act. Abolished the four-fold classification of states (Part A, B, C, D) and created 14 states and 6 union territories.

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Quick memory hooks to retain Article numbers and reorganisation committees.

items.title: Mnemonic 1
items.decryption: Union name & territory (Art 1), Admission of new external states (Art 2), Internal reorganization of existing states (Art 3), Simple majority rule/Schedules 1 & 4 amendments (Art 4).

items.title: Mnemonic 2
items.decryption: Chronological order of State Reorganisation Committees: Dhar Commission (1948) → JVP Committee (1948) → Fazl Ali Commission (1953).

items.title: Mnemonic 3
items.decryption: Remember that ceding territory requires a Constitutional Amendment (Art 368) as held in the Berubari Union Case (1960); simple Article 3 law is not enough.

items.question: What is the difference between 'Territory of India' and 'Union of India'?
items.answer: 'Territory of India' is a wider expression because it includes States, Union Territories, and acquired territories. 'Union of India' includes only the States.

items.question: Does Article 3 apply to the admission or establishment of new states that are not part of India?
items.answer: No. Article 3 deals with internal reorganization of existing states. Article 2 deals with the admission or establishment of new external states.

items.question: Is the prior recommendation of the President required for introducing an Article 3 bill in Parliament?
items.answer: Yes. An Article 3 bill can be introduced in either House of Parliament only on the prior recommendation of the President.

items.question: Is Parliament bound to accept the views of the state legislature concerned under Article 3?
items.answer: No. The President refers the bill to the state legislature for views, but Parliament is not bound by them and can accept or reject them.

items.question: What majority is required in Parliament to pass a state reorganization bill under Article 3?
items.answer: A Simple Majority. Article 4 explicitly states that such laws are not deemed amendments under Article 368.

traps.title: UPSC Civil Services Exam Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Confusing the scope of Article 2 and Article 3. Article 2 is for admitting or establishing new states that were *not* previously part of Indian territory. Article 3 is strictly for reorganizing states *already* within the territory of India.

Trap 2: Believing that ceding Indian territory to a foreign state can be done by a simple majority law under Article 3. The Supreme Court ruled in the Berubari Union case (1960) that ceding territory requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368.

Trap 3: Thinking that the views of a State Legislature under Article 3 are binding on Parliament. They are purely advisory. Parliament can proceed even if the State Legislature rejects the bill or fails to express views within the specified time.

sections.title: 1. Article 1 & 2 - Union of States & Admission/Establishment of New States
sections.content:
Article 1: Name and Territory of the Union

Article 1 states: "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States." This highlights two elements: the name of the country (India/Bharat) and the polity structure (Union of States). The term 'Union' was preferred over 'Federation' by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar to clarify that the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement by the states, and no state has the right to secede from it.

Article 2: Admission or Establishment of New States

Article 2 grants Parliament two powers:

  • Power 1: The power to admit into the Union of India new states.
  • Power 2: The power to establish new states.

Crucially, Article 2 relates to the admission or establishment of states that are not part of the territory of India (e.g., the admission of Sikkim in 1975 under the 36th Amendment Act).

sections.title: 2. Article 3 - Alteration of Areas, Boundaries or Names of Existing States
sections.content:
Article 3: Internal Reorganisation

Article 3 authorizes Parliament to reorganize existing states. It can: form a new state by separation of territory, increase or diminish the area of any state, alter the boundaries of any state, or alter the name of any state. This represents the concept of India being an "indestructible Union of destructible states."

sections.title: 3. Article 4 & Evolution of States (Reorganisation Committees)
sections.content:
Article 4: Constitutional Exceptions

Article 4 declares that laws made under Article 2 (admission) and Article 3 (reorganization) are not to be deemed as constitutional amendments under Article 368. This means such laws can be passed by a simple majority (a majority of members present and voting) and through normal legislative procedure.

JVP Committee1948Nehru, Patel, Sitaramayya. Formally rejected language as base.
Fazl Ali Commission1953Accepted language, but rejected "one language-one state" rule.
States Reorganisation Act1956Abolished Part A, B, C, D states. Created 14 states and 6 UTs.

Ceding Territory & Land Swaps

  • Berubari Union Case (1960): Supreme Court ruled that Article 3 does not cover ceding Indian territory to a foreign power. It requires a Constitutional Amendment Act under Article 368.
  • Boundary Settlement: Settlement of boundary disputes does not require a constitutional amendment. It can be done by executive action as it does not involve cession.
  • 100th Amendment (2015): Passed to give effect to the acquiring of certain territories by India and transfer of certain other territories to Bangladesh (exchange of enclaves).
